chief_complaint: heartburn and sour taste in the mouth after meals
hpi_details: burning sensation behind the breastbone, starting 30-45 minutes after meals (especially fatty, spicy, or tomato-based food). Worse when lying down or bending over. Reports a sour/acid taste in the back of the mouth. Relieved temporarily by OTC antacids. No dysphagia, no odynophagia, no weight loss, no hematemesis, no chest tightness or shortness of breath.
ideas: thinks it is acid reflux (GERD) related to his diet and weight
concerns: worried that the constant acid is damaging his food pipe or could lead to cancer in the long term
expectations: wants stronger prescription medication and advice on lifestyle changes
medications: amlodipine 5mg OD, over-the-counter antacids as needed
social_hx: office manager, smoker (10 cigarettes/day), drinks 4-6 units of alcohol per week

clinical_knowledge.topic: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes starting a trial of daily Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) (e.g., omeprazole 20mg OD for 4-8 weeks), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: heartburn and sour taste in the mouth after meals

Key HPI features: burning sensation behind the breastbone, starting 30-45 minutes after meals (especially fatty, spicy, or tomato-based food). Worse when lying down or bending over. Reports a sour/acid taste in the back of the mouth. Relieved temporarily by OTC antacids. No dysphagia, no odynophagia, no weight loss, no hematemesis, no chest tightness or shortness of breath.
Objective/Exam findings: Needs weight/BMI check, abdominal examination, blood pressure monitoring.
Relevant background/PMH: hypertension (diagnosed 3 years ago), mild obesity
Current medications: amlodipine 5mg OD, over-the-counter antacids as needed
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: dysphagia or odynophagia, unintentional weight loss or GI bleeding (haematemesis, melena), or chest pain with exertion or radiating to the arm/jaw.
management_principles: Start trial of daily Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) (e.g., omeprazole 20mg OD for 4-8 weeks)
Educate on lifestyle changes (weight loss, smoking cessation, avoiding food 3 hours before sleep, elevating head of bed)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 48M with chronic postprandial heartburn and acid regurgitation, aggravated by fatty/spicy food and recumbency. Temporarily relieved by antacids. No red flag symptoms (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding). History of hypertension and smoking.
reference_soap.objective: Needs weight/BMI check, abdominal examination, blood pressure monitoring.
reference_soap.assessment: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). DDx: gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, esophageal dysmotility, coronary artery disease (less likely given typical reflux symptoms and lack of exertional chest pain).
reference_soap.plan: Start trial of daily Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) (e.g., omeprazole 20mg OD for 4-8 weeks). Educate on lifestyle changes (weight loss, smoking cessation, avoiding food 3 hours before sleep, elevating head of bed). Advise return if dysphagia, weight loss, or persistent symptoms occur.

learning_objectives: Elicit typical GERD symptoms (heartburn, acid regurgitation, aggravating factors)
Screen for upper GI alarm symptoms (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, bleeding)
Differentiate esophageal symptoms from cardiac-related chest pain
Counsel the patient on lifestyle modifications (smoking cessation, weight loss, dietary changes)

teaching.one_liner: Stomach acid flows back up into the oesophagus, causing a burning sensation behind the breastbone and a sour taste in the mouth.
red_flags: Dysphagia or odynophagia — alarm feature needing urgent endoscopy
Unintentional weight loss or GI bleeding (haematemesis, melena)
Chest pain with exertion or radiating to the arm/jaw — must exclude a cardiac cause first

must_ask.say: Does the burning start soon after you eat, especially fatty or spicy food?
Is it worse when you lie down or bend over?
Do you get a sour or acid taste at the back of your throat?
Do you ever have trouble swallowing, or does food feel like it's sticking?
Do you ever get chest tightness or shortness of breath with exertion, separate from the burning?
Do you smoke, and how much alcohol do you drink?
Have you noticed any weight loss or change in your appetite?
